subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INQUIRY INTO USE OF CHEMICAL PESTICIDES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my honour and privilege to present a petition on behalf of a number of residents of Hinton, Red Deer, and Edmonton, Alberta, who are indicating their concern about the increasing number of chemicals used as herbicides and insecticides which are being proven to have negative effects on human health. They charge that these chemicals also produce short and longterm harmful effects on non-target organisms in soil and water.
They are calling upon the House of Commons to initiate a full inquiry into the safety, testing, registration and regulation of the use of pesticides and the examination of alternative ways of controlling pests such as biological control and plant derived pesticides.

speechtext:

speakeroldname: Mr. Russell MacLellan (Cape Breton-The Sydneys) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext:
That this House condemn the Government for its repeated failures to protect Canadian sovereignty and economic independence as demonstrated by its weak and ineffectual efforts to oppose Opinion 256 of the United States Federal Energy Regulatory Commission with regard to transmission costs of Canadian gas, and by its compliant approach to permitting foreign takeovers of Canadian corporations and natural resources.
He said: Mr. Speaker, my Party has brought forward this motion in order to bring to the attention of the Government and Canadians the seriousness with which we hold this ruling by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission in the United States.
On December 8, 1986, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission in the United States gave an opinion, saying that the two-price system which was in place for the sale of Canadian natural gas to the United States was not effective. It stated that the demand charge, which was one of the two prices that were being passed along to the buyers of natural gas in the United States, could no longer be applied, and that the transportation charge in the demand charge that was being paid willingly by American buyers, must be paid. It essentially told the Canadian natural gas industry that it had to absorb this charge.
This decision was made in contravention of a previous decision by Canada's National Energy Board which set forward the principle and the procedure for the sale of natural
gas in accordance with internationally accepted regulatory principles.
This decision raises two very important issues. First, this change will result in an additional cost of between $140 million and $400 million to the natural gas industry in western Canada. Second, it is blatant interference with Canadian law and the Canadian regulatory process and will be devastating to the natural gas industry in western Canada.
Our Party objected to this opinion from the very beginning and was adamant that it was one of the most arbitrary and damaging decisions that the United States has ever made against Canadian commerce. We were prepared to accept the Government's undertaking that it would take action and make interventions in the United States.
However, on May 27, just a few days ago, we learned that the petition of the Canadian natural gas producers to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission in the United States had been denied and that the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission was going to proceed with this very damaging decision even after the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) sent letters to the President, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) sent letters to the Secretary of Energy in Washington, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) communicated with the United States Government.
We object to such treatment of the Canadian natural gas industry by the United States as well as to the lukewarm interest, at best, that the Government is taking in this very serious situation. Not only will there be a dramatic loss to western natural gas producers, it will be a great deal more difficult to finance future projects in the natural gas industry in western Canada.
The most ludicrous aspect of this issue is that the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission in the United States does not have the jurisdiction to take that action. That commission is in charge of transportation of natural gas through the pipelines. It does not have jurisdiction over exports and imports, which is the prerogative of the Secretary of Energy through the Economic Regulatory Agency in the United States.
I want to take a moment to explain the position of the Economic Regulatory Agency. In its order of May 15, 1986, permitting the import of natural gas into the United States under the two-part price arrangement that existed before the December 8 ruling of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, the ERA found that the contract terms including the two-part price structure would "result in a more competitive and market responsive arrangement" and are "therefore not inconsistent with the public interest".
The Energy Regulatory Agency, the body responsible for importing and exporting natural gas, is in total agreement with the procedure of the National Energy Board. The ERA went on to say in February, 1984:
The market, not government, should determine the price and other contract
terms of imported gas. U.S. buyers should have full freedom-along with
responsibility-for negotiating the terms of trade arrangements with foreign
June 1, 1987

sellers. The federal Government's prime responsibility in authorizing imports should be to evaluate the need for the gas and whether the import arrangement will provide the gas on a competitively priced basis for the duration of the contract while minimizing regulation impediments to a freely operating market.
There is a blatant disregard for the ruling and the opinion of the Economic Regulatory Agency in the United States by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, which does not have responsibility for the item on which it has passed a judgment which completely counteracts the ruling of our own National Energy Board.
The National Energy Board suggested to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission that it would be an appropriate course of action for the commission to continue its previous practice of allowing the pass-through, to U.S. interstate pipeline rates, of those elements of cost which have been determined to be just and reasonable by a Canadian regulatory jurisdiction using internationally recognized toll marketing procedures. We thought reason would prevail in the United States, but that is not the case.
The United States Government has been completely oblivious to the urgency of the situation in Canada. The President of the United States is not living up to his commitment at the March, 1985, summit in Quebec City where the Prime Minister and the President agreed to work toward reducing trade restrictions and in particular to maintaining and extending open access to each other's energy markets.
On January 7, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources stated his objections to this decision in a speech in Los Angeles. Fie said that the FERC decision "raises serious questions of extraterritoriality, the extension of U.S. regulatory practices to matters under Canadian jurisdiction".
On the first day of the Prime Minister's tour in which he was trying to appease western Canadians, he stated that on May 5 he had written to the President about the seriousness of this situation and that the decision of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission on December 8 extended U.S. regulations into Canada. He asked the President to attempt to find a solution to this particular problem.
On May 27, the commission in the United States turned down the application of natural gas producers to overturn this very damaging decision.
There is complete disregard in the United States for the Government of Canada. The Americans are downplaying the intervention of American agencies into the laws of Canada. When the National Energy Program was in place the American Government stated that it wanted a level playing field. We are seeing the Government of the United States tilting the playing field to its advantage. That is not acceptable to Canadians in the west or anywhere else in Canada. It should not be acceptable to the Government.
There exists a freely negotiated contract between Canadian producers of natural gas and American buyers of natural gas whereby American buyers agreed to accept this toll charge as
Supply
part of the price of the natural gas. These were freely negotiated contracts under a regulatory framework, set up and approved by the National Energy Board, the law-making regulatory body in Canada with jurisdiction over this particular business.
We have a blatant overturning of Canadian laws as they affect Canada in Canada by an American regulatory commission. To me, this is the most damaging breach of Canadian sovereignty we have experienced in this country to date. In my opinion, and in the opinion of the Liberal Party, this is something which the Government cannot treat in a lukewarm fashion. It must daily use its most determined efforts to have this breach of Canadian identity overturned by the American Government.
How did this all come about? It came about, of course, largely because of the American Government's disregard for matters of Canadian interest and for the thinking of the Canadian Government. It also came about because the Government had to do away with the adjacent border price which assured Canadians that natural gas would be sold in the United States at a price not lower than the price for which it sold in Canada. The Government did away with that so it could sell natural gas into the United States more cheaply than it could sell it to Canadians. The American Government then panicked, the Americans panicked, and this is the result.
Just a little over a month after the federal Government did away with the adjacent border price this derogatory ruling was made by a United States commission, and it is going to be severely damaging to the Canadian economy. We were warned this was going to happen. We were warned by Mr. Dick Cahoon, spokesman for the 11,000 member Petroleum Marketers Association of America. He said, "This is unfair competition to do away with the adjacent border price". But, no, this Government, which legislates on energy by the seat of its pants, was completely oblivious to what was going on. As usual, energy was not a priority. Political will was not of interest.
The Prime Minister is now saying he is going to bring up this important issue at the Venice Summit. The Venice Summit will be held over two weeks after the turndown of the petition of the Canadian Natural Gas Producers to have this overturned. Nothing would be done for two weeks.
It is another issue which will be brought up in the negotiations. I will tell you, Madam Speaker, and I will tell this Government, that the Americans are taking energy seriously. They are taking the lack-lustre position of the Canada seriously. They look upon Canada as an energy fiefdom for their own interests. I do not object to the Americans wanting assistance from Canada for their energy needs and security of supply. However, I do object to the fact that we get kicked in the teeth, that we are supposed to provide everything the United States wants in the assurance of its own energy needs.

June 1, 1987
Supply
On May 6, just three weeks before the decision not to allow the appeal of the natural gas producers, President Reagan submitted, as one of his recommendations to Congress on the energy and national security concerns relating to oil import levels, that one of his concerns was "promoting the importance of stockpiles among U.S. allies". He was going to be doing this at Ministerial meetings of the International Energy Agency and at the Venice Economic Summit. So the President of the United States will be there telling his allies, including Canada, of the importance of stockpiling energy, particularly oil, so that this will be available to the United States.
At the same time, he is ignoring the very sovereignty of Canada in relation to energy, a matter in respect of which this Government has appealed time and again in a lack-lustre fashion-a little letter asking, "Oh, will you please, if you get time, look at this situation"-not giving it the urgency which it requires and which the Canadian people expect. This cannot go on. It just gets worse and worse.
The authority of Canada with regard to its trading partners, particularly the United States, is diminishing at a rapid rate. We are constantly doing what is wanted of us by the United States in order to secure a free trade agreement. A free trade agreement would be nice if it could be achieved without giving away the country. The Prime Minister, in his speech at the Economic Club in New York in December of 1984, said that Canada is open for business. But as the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) has said, Canada is not for sale.
It seems that in the opinion of foreign countries Canada is for sale, and it is for sale again and again. That is being proven each day by the treatment we are receiving from supposed friends such as the United States, from the takeover of companies such as Cadillac-Fairview, which is being purchased by a Chicago based company for $2.7 billion, and from the sale of Dome Petroleum to Amoco Canada, a 100 per cent owned subsidiary of Amoco Corporation in Chicago. There is no way that this can continue if we are going to have a free trade agreement, because there will be nothing left on this side of the border with which to enter into a free trade agreement.
Over the weekend, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) was very supportive of Amoco's position with respect to its offering of Canadian shares, but we do not know any of the details. We see that other bids cannot possibly be put forward by other companies who have signed a confidentiality agreement with Dome Petroleum. It seems that what is going on is whatever is wished by the American Government. We in this House are told that when we say these things we are being anti-American. This Party is not antiAmerican. What we are is pro-Canadian. This is something the Government should be. The Government is representing the interests of this country. These interests must not only be upheld, they must be maintained in the interests of this generation and future generations. They are not to be given away at fire sale prices'to the United States or any other country. These are resources which are in the interests of all of
Canada, and I ask the Government, for a change, to please represent and stick up for the rights of Canadians.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Masse (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with great interest to the views put forward by the Hon. Member for Cape Breton- The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan).
I noticed that in stating his position, the Hon. Member was careful not to mention the disastrous impact the Liberal Party's energy policies have had on the Canadian economy, especially in Western Canada.
Madam Speaker, everyone in this House knows perfectly well that under the National Energy Program, the previous Government, the Liberals under Pierre Elliott Trudeau, managed to drain billions of dollars of potential investment from the energy economy.
We remember the harm done to Canada's reputation in the international investment community, as a result of the protectionist and discriminatory barriers erected against our friends and allies in the western world.
No one will forget the profound alienation of Western Canada as a result of this policy.
We know too well the great damage that the National Energy Program caused the country. As a direct consequence of the NEP the country lost billions of dollars in potential investment. How many new jobs, how many new drilling starts, how much new exploration and development could have been achieved with these billions? We will never know.
Because of the National Energy Program an estimated $10 billion was lost to the petroleum economy through the petroleum and gas revenue tax. The PGRT, as we know, was one of the prime components of the NEP. We will never know what could have been done with that $10 billion which was taken directly from the petroleum companies because of the National Energy Program.

The Hon. Member claims the Government has been unable to protect Canada's sovereignty and economic independence. Madam Speaker, nothing could be further from the truth.
The Hon. Member says the Government has taken an accommodating approach to let foreign interests take over this country's companies and natural resources. That is of course not the case. This Government's approach is not the kind of unfortunate and inflexible attitude taken by the previous Government. It is flexible and tries to strike a balance between new investment, promoting the exploration and development of
June 1, 1987

our oil and gas resources and protecting what has been achieved in the way of Canadianization.
It is a policy that has been and continues to be favourable to Canada's economic interests, both in terms of the oil industry and the industrial structure of this country.
In December 1985, this Government approved a policy for foreign investment in the upstream component of the oil industry. Its objective was to encourage 50 per cent Canadian ownership in the oil sector by means of measures that would be flexible, market responsive and mindful of the need for encouraging investment.
Our acquisition policy for the oil and gas sector is quite clear. It allows the acquisition of companies already controlled by foreign interests, subject to Canadianization and investment commitments. Second, it does not allow the acquisition of financially sound Canadian companies by other companies controlled by foreign interests.
Third, it provides for considering the acquisition of Canadian-controlled companies in obvious financial difficulty.
This policy has proved a success. Canadian ownership has increased significantly since 1984-by about 5.5 per cent since the present Government came to power in 1984 and introduced this policy. Canadian ownership was stable at 42.5 per cent in 1984, and now, in 1986, it is 48 per cent. This means that our flexible policy that strikes a balance between investment and Canadianization has born fruit, so that now, 48 per cent of the industry is Canadian-owned.
We are of course anxious to see these developments continue, and I am sure that under this Government, the trend in the long term will be very positive. However, we have to acknowledge that we may be faced with losses as well as profits, especially in times of restructuring the industry or lower international prices, as has happened quite recently.
That is the Government's general policy. Now in the particular case of Dome, here again, we have to strike a balance between our Canadianization objective and our objective to increase exploration and development in this sector. It is no use saying that our natural resources belong to us, if we do not have a policy to develop them. What the Government is seeking is to have a balanced investment policy to ensure that these natural resources which belong to, and are the heritage of, Canadians are developed in the best interests of Canadians and our industry.
Let us first consider the facts in the Dome affair. We must remember that the majority of the company's shares are held by foreign interests. Nearly 57 per cent of Dome shareholders are non-Canadian. In addition, Dome has a special place in the oil industry. It is the second largest company in terms of upstream revenue. It is the biggest landowner in Western Canada. It ranks first on the number of its gas reserves and seventh for its oil reserves. It has become the largest gas
Supply
producer and the third largest producer of oil and hydrocarbons. With 4,000 employees, Dome is a major employer.
But the problem is that Dome is saddled with a $6.3 billion debt. Recently it reported losses of $2 billion, the biggest loss in the economic history of Canada. Of course everybody considers that Dome is now in a catrastophic financial situation. As a result of its financial woes Dome is severely restricted in its day-to-day operations. It has been and still is unable to make the investments required to maintain its assets, the kind of investments needed to carry out various projects in the territories for which it holds permits.

In the particular case of Dome it is important to seek a balance between our Canadianization objective and our objective to increase exploration and development in the industry. First, let us consider the facts. Dome is not a totally owned Canadian company. About 57 per cent of Dome's shareholders are foreigners. Dome has a very significant position in the industry. It is the second-largest company in terms of upstream revenues. It is the largest land holder in western Canada. It is the largest holder of gas reserves and the seventh-largest holder of oil reserves. It is the second-largest producer of gas and the third-largest producer of oil and field liquids. It is a large employer. About 4,000 people work for Dome. But Dome has a debt of $6.3 billion. It has recently announced a loss of $2 billion, the largest single loss in Canadian history. Due to its financial difficulties Dome has been constrained in its normal business dealings. It cannot make the necessary investments in its properties.

Therefore it is imperative to find a satisfactory solution to the Dome problem if gas and petroleum activities are to continue in Western Canada. The company must simply get back on an even keel and be in a position to make promising investments in its assets. Dome creditors also need a solution to this problem which has remained unsolved for too long. And among those creditors I would include a number of small companies in Western Canada which are Dome suppliers.
The Government has been cautious in this complex case which may have many consequences. Obviously the Government has no intention of buying Dome, therefore it is up to the private sector to take the initiative. This does not in any way lessen the significance we attach to Dome, but we will not use public funds to solve a problem created by the private sector. We have taken this approach for the following reasons. First, let me remind you of the origin of Dome's indebtedness, now standing at $6.3 billion, as I said. This money was borrowed by Dome, not by the Government of Canada, and the money was loaned by banks, not by the Government. It stands to reason that any solution to the Dome problems will force lenders and company shareholders to admit that their investments and their loans are worth less than the purchasing price or their book value.

June 1, 1987
Supply
It is clear that this Government is not responsible for these business losses. I remind the House that it was the discriminatory policy of Marc Lalonde and the promotion of Canadiani-zation through billions of dollars in PIP grants that led Dome to embark upon an overly ambitious acquisitions strategy.
Dome is not a public company. While the company has indeed benefited from various tax and subsidy programs over the years, these have been policies of general application. The fact that it has received such public largesse, however, has led some to conclude that the Government has a special responsibility to protect creditors. My colleagues and I are determined that such will not be the case. We are not in favour of and will not support a bail-out disguised as a sale.
Our position has received public and media support. On May 12 The Toronto Sun editorial said:
The notion that Dome should be kept Canadian by accepting a poorer offer is patently absurd. If Amoco or someone else can somehow turn Dome around and make rescue a reality, perhaps some Canadians should sit up and take notice.
The Financial Times on April 27 said:
For a refreshing change the Canadian Government seems content to play a minimalist role, surely the proper one under the circumstances.
On May 8 the Gleaner of Fredericton, New Brunswick, contained these words:
Government meddling in the oil and gas industry in recent years has been so costly that the people of this country should be skeptical of the interventionist views over Dome Petroleum.

Madam Speaker, Members of the Opposition have been urging us to intervene to seal the outcome of the Dome purchase offer. They suggested that the Government should use its clout and make sure that a Canadian company be favoured. Madam Speaker, this suggestion reveals their ignorance of the law: there simply is not a Canadian law under which the Government would be able to give the nod to a Canadian bidder. Dome belongs to its shareholders, not to the Government. The Government has set a clear and no-strings-attached framework for companies anxious to do business in Canada. Pursuant to this process any offer, including Amoco's, must be examined in light of the legislation and policies prevailing in this country. Any other approach would make it mandatory for the Government to pass specific new legislation in this case, and this would have a strong negative impact on investments, on quality, on our country's image and, ultimately, on job creation.

The results of establishing this clear framework can now be seen. Dome's problems are well under way to being resolved. We have witnessed a healthy competitive process which is in the interests of all Parties, be they employees, suppliers, shareholders or creditors.
There have been three bids to acquire Dome, one from a Canadian firm. To date a foreign firm, Amoco, has made the best bid which was selected by the Dome board of directors. No one has denied that that is the case. However, the deal has not yet been approved by Dome's creditors and shareholders. Other companies have indicated a continued interest in Dome.

If Amoco's bid is approved by Dome creditors and shareholders, then the acquisition will have to be reviewed by Investment Canada. The Government which I represent wants to make sure that such a purchase will be of significant benefit to Canada. I have already said I am convinced that such a company will have to be a model organization for corporate citizens. It is very important that any company seeking a merger abide by high standards with respect to investment, job creation and Canadian ownership. Madam Speaker, we would be acting irresponsibly if we were to engage in public negotiations concerning this kind of takeover. Still I can assure you that this Government is intent on making sure that the deal be in the interests of Canada.
No official request has been submitted to the Government as yet, but we have taken some significant measures to guarantee that Amoco's proposal, if it goes through all the required stages, is a profitable one for Canada.
I had a meeting with Amoco executives at my office, and I let them know, in the clearest possible terms, how important the Government felt this transaction to be and that we would ensure it would benefit Canadians in terms of jobs, investment and participation in the company.
Last week, Mr. Dan Stacey, President of Amoco Canada, announced that his corporation would issue a substantial number of shares in Canada, if the proposal to purchase Dome Petroleum was accepted. Thus the principle of Canadian participation in the development of our oil and gas resources will be respected. It also guarantees that the corporation will have a Canadian face. Madam Speaker, I believe this was a major decision. For the first time in its corporate existence, Amoco has agreed to create a local corporation in a country outside the United States, and I think that the discussions and the Government's position, as expressed in the clearest possible terms by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, were instrumental in convincing Amoco that there were certain requirements that had to be met to do business in Canada.

This is a major commitment on the part of Amoco, one which should be commended. It will mark the first time in 40 years that Canadians will have an opportunity to participate directly as shareholders in the company's growth. As I indicated to Amoco, I believe Canadians should have a right to invest directly in the development of their resources. This is particularly important in the case of a company which, by a number of measures, would be the largest oil and gas firm operating in Canada.
June 1, 1987



I would now like to address the first example given in the motion, which deals with the action taken by the Canadian Government subsequent to Opinion 256 of the United States Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.
First of all, I must say I am surprised to see the Opposition take an interest in negotiations on the sale of natural gas to the United States. I find this sudden turnaround particularly surprising when 1 recall, and with me the oil industry in Western Canada, that dismal period from 1980 to 1984, when the Government at the time, formed by the Liberal Party to which the Lion. Member belongs, imposed its energy policy in such a cavalier fashion. The arbitrary and tyrannical measures adopted unilaterally by the Liberal Government provided for setting the price of Canadian natural gas without consideration for American market criteria. They also gave us an unenviable reputation as a country that could not be trusted to be a reliable and reasonable trading partner.
[English)
Needless to say, the New Democratic Party's approach to energy trade is simply to shut it down. The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) admits that in 1979 the NDP passed a resolution calling for an end to natural gas exports. He now says his Party's policy is that there should be "reasonable" gas exports, whatever that means. He cannot have it both ways; supporting gas exports when he is in the West and opposing them when he is in the East. It is time now for the NDP to make up its mind and let the people of Canada know what its energy policy really is. Do they or do they not favour the export of natural gas?

Nevertheless, we have at least one motive for rejoicing. The Opposition has finally realized the importance of the natural gas trade between Canada and the United States. At least, I find something positive in this change of heart and I can tell the Opposition outright that Opinion 256 represents a serious threat for the trade deals which, over the past 30 years, have been beneficial to both Canadians and Americans.
The FERC Opinion defines the manner in which American corporations can recoup from their customers the costs of purchasing Canadian natural gas. This decision was officially made public on December 8, 1986, and confirmed on May 27, 1987. The Opinion prohibits the full recovery of some costs from American customers. These are the costs which had been borne in Canada and set by Canadian regulating agencies to provide pipe-line corporations with the capacity to serve export markets.
In practice, FERC will make it possible to by-pass transmission costs set in Canada, but only from the American point of view.
We foresee that the yearly difference between the actual costs assumed by exporters and the recovery carried out by
Supply
FERC will amount to at least SI40 million US per year. According to FERC, our own producers should carry this burden, and we are greatly concerned about this.
The Government sees in this Opinion, first a foreign intrusion in the regulatory jurisdiction of a Canadian agency, second an unfair tax burden imposed on the Canadian natural gas producing industry and, third, a significant set back from the joint efforts of Canada and the United States to establish a bilateral market oriented energy trade.
The motion before the House describes the Canadian response to this Opinion as "weak and ineffectual". It is not, Madam Speaker. On September 4, when the FERC Opinion had not yet been finalized, I met in Washington with Mr. Herrington, the American Secretary of Energy, and expressed my concern about this Opinion. This meeting marked the beginning of a concerted offensive by the producing provinces, the Canadian natural gas industry and my Cabinet colleagues to make the U.S. authorities more aware of the impact of this Opinion on the natural gas trade which brings wealth to both our countries.
I think it is important to enlighten the House about our initiatives. On December 18, together with my Alberta and British Columbia counterparts, I sent a note to the Secretary of State expressing our views and concerns about Opinion 256.
The exporting companies, the main associations of Canadian producers, the National Energy Board and the provinces' regulating agencies have all made official representations to FERC seeking new hearings.
In February, the officials of the Alberta Government and those in my Department advised fully their Canadian counterparts in the Ministries of Energy and Trade. My Cabinet colleagues, including the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), the Minister for International Trade (Mrs. Carney) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) have all had official discussions concerning this issue with their opposite numbers in the United States.
Opinion 256 was discussed during the Canada-United States Summit with took place here in Ottawa last March. Finally, on May 5, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) wrote the President of the United States to express our country's concern about the impact of this Opinion.
Unfortunately, these concerted efforts have failed so far in convincing FERC to amend its decision. But we should keep in mind that this organization is an independent regulatory agency which must act within the limits of its mandate as determined by laws and regulations.
In spite of the fact that we may very well have lost the first innings, Madam Speaker, we have not yet lost the game, and the representatives of private corporations are already determined to bring the whole issue before the courts, and they can count on the support of this Government, especially the Department of Energy, because this decision of our American

June 1, 1987
Supply
friends is contrary to the interests of both American and Canadian consumers.

Madam Speaker, I am afraid the Minister has not convinced those of us on this side of the House of the Government's sincerity in terms of pressing the matter as hard as it possibly can and giving it the attention it deserves.
What has the Minister done since the request by the producers of Canadian natural gas to have the ruling of FERC overturned? Since the decision was handed down on May 27, has the Minister contacted his counterpart in the United States? Has he arranged for meetings with the Secretary of Energy in the United States? Has the Prime Minister been in contact with President Reagan?
This is not an ordinary discussion on a subject of mutual interest; this is a discussion on something of vital importance to the United States. To say that it can go through the courts is not enough. It could be tied up for years in the courts.

Madam Speaker, first we did not hide the seriousness of the situation. We have publicly expressed our dissatisfaction with the decision. But we must respect the American legal system. It is the same kind of system that we ourselves recognize in Canada.
The National Energy Board can make decisions that may not always please the Government, but such is life, and that is the kind of system we chose to establish in Canada and in the United States.
But as a Minister of Energy, I and the Government as such made known our dissatisfaction with a decision that in our view is not in the best interests of Canadians and of American consumers.
Second, we have been in constant and frequent contact with the private sector, and we support their move to take that decision to the U.S. courts.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to refer to a press release dated May 6 issued by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in Alberta. He indicated that the Government was concerned about the potential ruling to which the Minister referred. He said that the Minister had been in touch with his American counterparts, that a variety of cabinet Ministers had been in touch with their counterparts in the U.S., and that he had been in touch with the United States President.
Will the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) now admit that despite all the overtures-his best efforts, the best efforts of the Prime Minister and of his colleagues-that all their requests fell on deaf ears? Will he admit that the Americans said, "No, we are not going to pay any attention. We are going to go ahead and do exactly what we want to do in Canada?"

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member knows the American system better than that. We in Canada accept that the judiciary power is something different from the administration. Let us be honest. We have discussed that case with our counterparts in the United States. I have met many times- and the last time was two weeks ago-with the Secretary of Energy in the United States. I can tell the Hon. Member that they have agreed to the basic principles on which we are working-to have a freer market and so on and to make sure that consumers in both countries will be pleased by our policy. However, that does not give him the right to direct the judiciary power in the United States.
The same applies in Canada. It may happen in Canada that Governments agree with a foreign Government about a situation, but that does not give the Prime Minister the right to telephone a judge somewhere and say, "You have to do this because the political power of the country has decided that that is the way it should be done". If we did that in Canada, the Hon. Member's Party would be the first to say that we do not respect the way Governments are organized.
I think we have to recognize that the United States has the right to be organized on the same democratic principles as us. That does not mean that the Government of the United States disagrees with the Government of Canada. If a judge or a board of judges decided something contrary to the will of the American administration, the next step would be to appeal and to fight in court. That is not a political decision. That is not a decision of the administration of the United States. It is a decision of the judiciary power.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I completely disagree with the Minister of Energy. This is not only hurting the economy of western Canada and the country as a whole, but it is an infringement of Canadian laws. It is an extension of U.S. regulations into Canada, which is completely unacceptable. Also, we have FERC exercising a decision on something over which it does not have jurisdiction, the import-export of natural gas.
Surely the Minister in his discussions with the Secretary of Energy in the United States has brought to the Secretary's attention that this is his jurisdiction, not the jurisdiction of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. The Minister should be doing something to support his own position.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have no difficulty in agreeing with my colleague. That is exactly what we have said publicly. The decision is contrary to the interests of both, and is an intrusion in our own regulatory responsibility. We have said that. The Hon. Member says nothing that we do not support. We said it before the Liberals and we have said it publicly. In the United States and everywhere we have said that it is not acceptable.
We agree with that, but that does not give my colleague, Mr. Herrington, the right to phone the judge and say, "You
June 1, 1987

are wrong and you will do it another way". He cannot do that. He has no right. The Hon. Member knows that Mr. Herrington has no right to do that.
I have no right to instruct the National Energy Board on such issues when it is the board independently that must take a decision. We have to accept that. We can be annoyed with the American system and its decision, and I fully agree that we should be annoyed. But we cannot force the United States of America into changing its basic democratic system. It is, by the way, the same as the one we have in Canada.
The Liberal Party will never agree to the Minister of Energy, or the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) phoning CRTC giving them a directive. I have to respect our system. I am doing that as a Minister. The least I can do is accept that my colleague has roughly the same approach in the United States and I must respect him. As far as having a discussion, we agree, but that does not give the Secretary of Energy the right to instruct the judge.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, when the Minister of Energy wanted to test and have an examination of the surplus natural gas in Canada he wrote to the National Energy Board asking for hearings and the board held hearings. If the Secretary of Energy's position through the economic regulatory agency in the United States is being usurped, the Minister has a right to do something about it. Do something; at least call the Secretary of Energy, write him a letter. Maybe without a stamp the letter may get to the Secretary anyway, but just do something.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am surprised that my hon. colleague forgets that that is exactly what happened. The Americans have announced a review of their tariff in the United States. That issue, we are sure, will be part of their study. So that is already done. We did not have to wait for the Liberal Party to discover that. There will be a board in the United States to review the tariff. It is done.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, would the Minister explain why the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) bothered writing to the President of the United States if he felt that he could not really intervene because it was a judicial decision rather than an administrative or political decision? Why did the Prime Minister happen to write to the President just the day before he went to Red Deer, Alberta, and appeared with the oil rig people? Was it strictly grandstanding or did the Prime Minister hope to be able to intervene in the decision?
From what the Minister said, I take it that the Government disagrees with the United States administration, but is supporting private individuals going before the U.S. judicial system. Does the Government plan to take this matter to the international court because the United States is applying its laws, extraterritorially, into Canada? Is the Minister prepared to do that?
It seems to me that this decision sets a tremendous precedent which could be used in all kinds of other areas, especially
Supply
when the United States regulatory agency is agreeing with the decision while another department is disapproving of it. It seems to me that the Government should not lay down and play dead just because free trade negotiations are going on.
Has the Minister examined with his officials the economic impact and how many jobs this will involve? It occurs to me that the $400 million is about the same as the investment which the Government plans to give under the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program which the Government suggested might create some 15,000 or 20,000 jobs. Will this decision, if it stands-if the Government does not appeal it or does not have it overturned-cost us 15,000 jobs in that profits will be creamed off which will not be available for exploration and development? Can the Minister respond to those several questions?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext:
In that question, Madam Speaker, I see at least three sub-questions. First, there is an important distinction to be made between representations and instructions. What the Government did through the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, Government officials, even provinces and the Prime Minister and my colleagues, was to make representations, explain the situation. The American system provides for an opportunity to make representations before such a tribunal, in the same way as before the CRTC or the National Energy Board, people can make representations, and the U.S. Administration on behalf of the Canadian Government made a number of representations.
This is the difference between making representations and giving instructions to the legal system, and I believe my hon. colleague in his question recognizes there is a distinction, that we must respect the legal system both in United States and Canada.
Second problem-should the matter be brought before international tribunals? I believe the first step, according to the lawyers in charge of that matter, is first and foremost to bring the case before the American courts. If and when a review and recommendations lead us to believe there are other legal avenues, you can rest assured the Canadian Government will act to support our industry wherever needed. This I can assure my hon. colleague.
Third, the estimated amounts are in the order of $140-150 million rather than the order you mentioned. Of course, such evaluations are always difficult to make, but it is the evaluation that was made available to us and that will be largely supported by exporters. How many jobs would be lost because of lack of investment resulting from the loss of those $140 million? I have no figures at the moment. That may happen in some cases. Hopefully, the number of jobs that will be lost as a result of that decision will be kept to a minimum. It may happen-but how many? Certainly not in the orders you referred to, because the initial amount itself is not in the order you mentioned earlier.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, as Canadians looked at their newspapers over the weekend and again this morning, they saw in almost every newspaper in Canada headlines such as, "Disaffected westerners spawn new federal political Party". That description was not quite right because when you look at who were those westerners meeting in Vancouver this past weekend you will see that they were almost exclusively Conservatives. As a matter of fact, the largest contingent was from Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext: I saw some disappointed New Democrats.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext:
When you look through the list, 95 per cent were card carrying members of the Conservative Party. They said that they have been betrayed by the Conservatives, and they feel that the only way to register their concern, after sending the largest majority of westerners to the House of Commons hoping that their views would be put on the parliamentary table, and now having been abandoned by the P.C. Government, is to form their own political Party. I think that speaks clearly for itself.
Today we discuss another betrayal of western Canadians and a betrayal of Canadians generally. More and more when people try to determine what the future of Canada holds they will not be paying attention to what is going on on Parliament Hill, they will be looking at Congress. Decisions being made in the United States are having increasingly more impact on the future for our country. When asked to test the Cruise missile, the Government said yes, let's test the Cruise missile. When the Americans wanted to take over West Kootenay Power and Light Company, the Government said yes. When they wanted to have a 10-year monopoly on American drugs being sold in Canada, they were given that right. When they wanted to take over Dome Petroleum, the Government gave them the right to take over Dome Petroleum. When they wanted to impose a special tax on Canada's softwood lumber industry, that was fine. As a matter of fact, the Canadian Government itself imposed that 15 per cent tax to keep Canadian wood out of the United States.
In this weekend's newspaper, there was a report from the National Forest Products Association of America indicating that the new tax imposed by Canada has achieved what it was intended to do, it has kept Canadian wood out of the United States market. As a matter of fact, Canada's share of the United States market slipped to 28.7 per cent in the first two months of 1987, down from 31.5 per cent a year earlier. Now the United States does not even have to pass its own laws to keep goods from coming from Canada. The Government of Canada will do it for it. This is nothing short of a betrayal.
Over the last few days a former Prime Minister has spoken about the Meech Lake Accord and has called the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) a weakling. Indeed, we could consider to what extent the Prime Minister has betrayed Canada. A few weeks ago, the Prime Minister went from place to place in western Canada saying, "We will fight the Americans on this gas issue, we are concerned". Well, some fighter. That was like the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) when she was sitting on the beaches of Maui saying, "We will fight the softwood issue, we will fight them on the beaches of Hawaii, we will stop the Americans". Yet the Government imposed its own tax on the softwood producers of Canada.
Maybe the best thing that could happen to us is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) not to speak to his counterparts in the United States, for the rest of the cabinet Ministers including the Minister for International Trade not to speak to their United States counterparts and for the Prime Minister not to phone or write letters to Mr. Reagan any longer. Whenever he does this on our behalf, we are betrayed. We are sold out.
As the speaker from the Liberal Party indicated when the American-good grief, I was going to say when the American Prime Minister-when the Canadian Prime Minister was in the United States saying that Canada was now open for business, what he meant was that it is now for sale. In two and a half years we have seen more foreign transactions and takeovers in our economy than in any other similar period in history. In fact, there have been 2,200 foreign transactions, primarily takeovers by American companies. We are now seeing more intrusion than ever.
I respect the honesty of the Minister of Energy. On many occasions he speaks forthrightly. Last Thursday, he said that the implementation of this rule will extend the United States regulation into Canada. Indeed, I appreciate his point. The United States is now deciding how we should export our natural gas. The United States is now determining our export policy for natural gas, just as it is now deciding how we should impose softwood lumber stumpage rates in the various provinces.
I think it is time the Parliament of Canada said something about this. It will have the opportunity to do so today as a result of this Opposition Motion. Parliamentarians ought to say that it is time Parliament started determining our economic policies, not the Congress or the quasi-judicial bodies in the United States.
Let me identify the extent of this natural gas disaster for western Canada. Perhaps as much as $400 million will be lost as a result of the Government's inability to deal effectively with the United States in ensuring a movement of Canadian exports to the U.S. The United States has indicated its concern about this incredible wave of Canadian natural gas invading its markets. What a peculiar view considering that between 4 per cent and 5 per cent of the United States' demand is met by Canada. As a matter of fact, in the last few months there has
June 1, 1987

been a 17 per cent decline in exports to the United States. When the Americans talk about unfair competition from Canada, perhaps we should ask them to explain why there has been a 17 per cent drop in exports over the last number of months.
I recognize that 30 per cent of our natural gas is exported, giving us a $2.5 billion revenue flow.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext: Where do you stand on that?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext: If I were that person from Alberta, 1 would not be here today. I would be going door to door in my constituency because-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext: Where do you stand on the export of natural gas? Just answer that.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext:
He is presumably asking where I or my Party stand on the export of natural gas. After our security has been declared, then we are certainly in favour of exports of natural gas. However, let us take care of Canada first.
Conservative Members are laughing at me when I say we should take care of Canadian concerns first. Of course they laugh. After giving away most of Canada since they have been in office for two and a half years, anything that puts Canada first would be a laughing matter to the Conservatives. As I say, I would advise them to get to their constituencies to try to explain why once again they have agreed to betray western Canadian concerns regarding the export of natural gas.
Things will be changing very shortly. I think Canadians have had enough. They have indicated that they will not stand by and watch the situation deteriorate continuously over the years. They have registered that at the polls where they have indicated clearly right across Canada that they are now turning their backs on Progressive Conservatives, having seen what they have been able to do to Canada, particularly to western Canada.
As the Minister of Energy has indicated, the decision of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission in Washington will now result in Americans extending their regulations into Canada. Over the last while, part of the cost of transmission of natural gas in Canada was reflected in the price obtained by natural gas companies. We have been doing that with the United States and, as a matter of fact, there have been negotiations going on with the United States to ensure that the free flow of natural gas into the United States market to serve American consumers would continue. This system has been working well for years and years. All of a sudden the Americans have presumably decided that 4 per cent or 5 per cent of the market being supplied by Canadian gas is too much and therefore they need to take steps to reduce the flow southward. That is exactly what they have done.
In spite of the efforts of the Prime Minister to reverse this decision, nothing of the sort has occurred. We will now have to rely on the consortium of natural gas exporters to take this matter to court in the United States in an attempt to oppose it.
Supply
Obviously the Government has failed in its efforts. The Cabinet has failed in its efforts. The Minister of Energy has failed in his efforts. Now a court action by a consortium of natural gas exporters will be required to attempt to reverse this decision, in co-operation, I might add, with American consumers. They too are concerned. They thought they were getting a good deal because Canadian exports of natural gas provided competition and kept prices down. As a result of this decision, it is unknown what will happen to competitive pricing.
Let us turn for a moment or two to the matter of foreign ownership. I think it is disgraceful that in spite of all the warnings about the tremendously high levels of foreign investment in Canada and, more importantly, the role of foreign control in our economy, Canada has more of its economic decisions made in foreign countries than any other country in the world. The board offices in Tokyo, Dallas, New York and Chicago will be making decisions on corporate investment and expansion in Canada for the next 10 years.
In the last two and a half years since the Conservative administration took office, Investment Canada has approved hundreds and hundreds of foreign takeovers. Considering that, we must ask what we are getting for those takeover dollars that are presumably coming to Canada.
It was revealed last week that of all the foreign investment which has come into Canada in the last two and one-half years 95 per cent has been used for takeovers; not new plants or the opening of new mines or factories, but for takeovers. As a result of this incredible dominance by a foreign presence in our economy a lot of money leaves Canada every week and goes back to the head offices. In fact, every day, seven days a week, 52 weeks a year, $2.5 million each hour flows out of Canada back to the parent companies in other countries, primarily in the United States of America. One of the major reasons there is a lot more investment in Canada is because every hour of the day $2.5 million flows out of Canada back to foreign countries. No other country in the world accepts this state of affairs.
How is it in Canada's best interest to have such extensive foreign involvement in our economy? The most recent example is the Dome takeover. Amoco has operated in Canada for 40 years. In spite of the length of time during which it has been here there is not a single Canadian on its board of directors and there is absolutely no Canadian ownership whatsoever. This company now wants to take over one of the critical players in the oil and gas industry of Canada.
The Government favours an American company taking over Dome Petroleum; it approves an American company having total control of this company and that future profits made in Canada will go to the United States.
Where do we turn to when we have a Government which thinks it is a great idea to have foreigners deciding our future? We can only hope that the people of Canada will realize that there is an incredible sell-out taking place and will register

June 1, 1987
Supply
their concern in the next federal election. Unfortunately, that will probably not come for 18 months and in the interim we must do what we can to bring some logic to the Dome takeover.
We believe there are alternatives. The proposal that Dome would sell some of its shares to Canada if the Amoco takeover is approved is of little comfort. It is important to distinguish clearly between ownership and control. We are concerned that the control of Dome will be held by foreigners, mainly Amoco representatives, rather than Canadians. The decision of where the parent company will be headquartered will, therefore, be made in the best interests of the United States. Handing out a few shares to Canadian shareholders will not change that one iota. The future decision-making of that company will be done by people who are not Canadian citizens. Presumably they will be good American citizens, so the decisions will be made in the best interests of the Amoco corporation and, ultimately, the United States of America.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext: The Tories don't mind that.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext:
As my friend from Ottawa says, the Tories don't mind that. Presumably this is what they want. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) went to New York and said that we want more foreigners doing business in Canada he was really saying that the Government does not have faith in Canadian investors and entrepreneurs. Well, Madam Speaker, we have faith. We believe that we should begin looking for solutions to job creation and economic prosperity at home. We should take pride in the knowledge that we can do the job and do not have to turn to the Japanese, Americans or Germans to solve our problems. We like their support, encouragement and involvement, but we are not looking to them to solve our economic problems.
The United States Federal Energy Regulatory Commission has indicated that it wants to change the rules under which we export our natural gas. It has said that the way in which we handle the transmission of our gas and assign the charges to that transmission is not now appropriate for exports to the United States.
This is a very short-sighted decision by the Americans. In 1986 we exported 744 billion cubic feet to the United States. That is a relatively small amount considering our historic trend. It was that low because of the fall in the cost of No. 6 fuel oil in the United States. I suspect that that is probably a temporary situation and that in the future the cost of No. 6 fuel oil will go up, as oil costs generally do. The demand for natural gas will then increase. As a matter of fact, only a few days ago western oil reports indicated that Tennaco from the United States was in Canada looking for possible ways to facilitate future gas exports to the United States.
We must also realize that President Reagan is a lame duck President. While our Prime Minister and the President of the United States may be good friends, write letters back and forth, and telephone each other as the news release indicates, it
is really Congress which decides upon the protectionist policies that will be applied.
As a result of this recent decision by FERC the playing field for natural gas exports to the United States has been tilted in favour of the U.S. They no longer provide equal opportunities for Canadian exporters- to the United States. That is the real concern. We must realize that because the Prime Minister calls President Reagan on a regular basis and asks for his help is irrelevant. The President of the United States is either not interested in intervening on Canada's behalf, or not prepared or not able to intervene on Canada's behalf. Whatever the reason, that the Prime Minister reminds us daily of his close friendship with President Reagan is of little comfort, indeed.
In closing, we once again find that western Canada has been betrayed by the inability of the Government to deal with the international crisis affecting natural gas exports, just as the Government was so woefully inadequate in its response to the challenge on softwood lumber exports. One almost shudders to think of what tomorrow's headline will bring us. On what sector will the Americans next make a demand in response to which the Government, true to form, will say that if there is any way in which we can co-operate we will do so, whether with regard to steel exports, agricultural or mineral policy? More than simply having caved in, the Government has cooperated with the American demand on Dome.
We oppose the way in which the Government has bungled the situation of natural gas exports. In spite of the promises made by the Prime Minister when he was in western Canada that he would do something, he has done nothing about this matter. In spite of the promises of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources that he would do something, he has done nothing. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources admitted today in the House that he was unable to do anything, that it is now up to the law courts in the United States and it will probably take years and years. It looks as though all Canadians will have to look to another political Party if their interests are to be adequately met.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). His opening and closing remarks seemed to sum up the purpose of his rising to speak in the House today. In my opinion, he is not really concerned about the problems that we face in the energy industry in western Canada, but concerned about his Party's popularity and opportunity to transfer some of the support that has supposedly eroded from the Conservative Party in midterm over to his Party.
I want to assure him that his rhetoric and misspeak will not go unnoticed. The Hon. Member talked about takeovers and that they represented a takeover of Canada by the United States. Of course, we in the House are familiar with the New Democratic Party rhetoric and that the socialist party of this country has always been anti-American.
June 1, 1987

The Member said that we allowed the Americans to come here and test the Cruise missile. We know the position of the socialist New Democratic Party about the NATO Alliance. Now they are trying to hide that policy and say that we have a commitment to defend the north. They are against armed forces in the north yet say we must defend and define our position in the north.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext: Come off it. We never said that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext: They are having difficulty determining their own position. They then talk about drugs. We are the only western country-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext:
Listen to them now. The socialists are speaking rhetoric, as they always do. Let us consider the drug question. We are the only western country that did not recognize and protect intellectual property.
The New Democrats say that we are allowing "those dirty Americans" to take over Dome Petroleum. Presently, Canadians own 25 per cent to 30 per cent of Dome. Amoco has offered to take over Dome to keep it operating and has said that it would sell off the same per centage of shares to Canadians. Now the New Democratic Party says that is not good enough, that there should be control of the company.
Let us consider the lumber issue. The Americans proposed a 25 per cent countervail duty on lumber going into the United States. We worked out an agreement and introduced a Bill that kept the money in Canada.
The speeches by the NDP are strictly anti-American rhetoric. They talked about Mr. Trudeau, the Constitution, and the Meech Lake Accord. Why did the New Democratic Party deny in the Constitution and the Bill of Rights that we passed in the House the right of each Canadian to own property?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext: We never did.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE
speechtext: They were shoulder to shoulder with Pierre Elliott Trudeau because they are socialists and cannot allow individual Canadians to own property. The New Democratic Party betrayed every Canadian because they prevented the inclusion of the right of ownership of property in the Constitution so that all Canadians and their children could have the fundamental right to own property. That is where the socialists stand.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SOVEREIGNTY AND ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE

Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) that his Party has been in government for almost three years. Have those Members indicated an interest in entrenching property rights in the Constitution?

We have been talking about the Constitution for months but they have never mentioned that the Government is at all interested in putting property rights in the Constitution.
I can understand why the Member is upset. I would be upset as well if I was part of a majority of 212 Members that had 60 per cent of the popular vote in Canada but is now at some 22 per cent. I would also be concerned because we know that Alberta will be changing its electoral behaviour significantly as soon as the opportunity arises.
The Hon. Member mentioned the Dome Petroleum takeover. Our Party is concerned about the Dome takeover because it plays a critical role in the natural gas and oil industry of Canada. It is a major player in the oil patch in western Canada and we believe that it ought to be maintained in Canadian hands. The majority of Canadians feel the same way, as in the testing of the Cruise. When it comes to the takeover of Dome by a foreign enterprise, most Canadians believe it is not in our best interests and would rather see a Canadian solution.
We proposed a Canadian solution, which involves a consortium of a number of Canadian companies, including Petro-Canada, that be allowed to make a bid to take over Dome Petroleum and keep it in Canadian hands. The Government has not shown any interest in such a proposal.
Day after day we urged the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to facilitate a Canadian solution, but he is not interested. The point that must be made is that the evidence over the last two and one-half years leads one to believe that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Government of Canada would prefer a foreign takeover to allow Americans to run the economy of Canada rather than Canadians.
That is clearly where we differ. We have faith in Canadians and in Canada. We want a Canadian solution and expected the Minister of Energy to facilitate a Canadian solution. He did not do so because the Government does not believe such a solution is useful either now or in the future.
When it comes to Canada, we in the New Democratic Party prefer a Canadian solution. We believe a Canadian solution is possible if the Government would allow Petro-Canada to work in consortium with a number of other Canadian companies to come forward with a Canadian bid for troubled Dome Petroleum.
